content: Amblyopia is a condition characterized by a reversible deficit in vision, which must be addressed during the sensitive period of visual development to achieve effective treatment outcomes. Screening programs have been established to identify this condition, which often presents without symptoms, and to refer affected children for treatment while there is still potential for visual improvement. However, the value of these screening programs and the optimal protocols for their implementation remain subjects of debate. The purpose of this review was to assess the effectiveness of vision screening programs in reducing the prevalence of amblyopia. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in several electronic databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (up to Issue 3, 2008), MEDLINE (from January 1950 to August 2008), and EMBASE (from January 1947 to August 2008). The last search was performed on August 15, 2008. No restrictions were applied regarding language, and no manual searches of journals were conducted. The review intended to analyze data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster-randomized trials that compared the prevalence of amblyopia in populations subjected to vision screening versus those that were not screened. Two independent authors reviewed the abstracts identified through the electronic searches. Full-text versions of relevant studies were obtained, and authors of studies were contacted when additional information was required. However, no data suitable for analysis were identified, and no meta-analysis could be performed. Despite the extensive body of literature available on vision screening, no trials were found that directly compared the prevalence of amblyopia in screened versus unscreened populations. This lack of evidence from randomized controlled trials makes it challenging to evaluate the impact of current vision screening programs on the prevalence of amblyopia. The absence of such evidence does not imply that vision screening is ineffective; rather, it indicates that this intervention has not yet been rigorously tested in well-designed trials. To enable such trials, it is necessary to establish normative data for age-appropriate vision tests and to reach a consensus on the definition of amblyopia. Furthermore, the long-term consequences of living with untreated amblyopia need to be quantified, and a comprehensive cost-benefit analysis of vision screening programs should be conducted.
